R.q: Read the passage. Select the sentence that best supports the conclusion that adding evening appointments did not reduce the clinic's overall rate of missed appointments.

parts.t: In January, Fairview Clinic began sending text reminders two days before each appointment.
In March, the clinic also added evening appointment times on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
The share of missed appointments fell from 18 percent in December to 9 percent in February.
From March through May, the share of missed appointments stayed at about 9 percent.
Patients who booked evening slots missed them less often than patients who booked morning slots.

sn.a: In January, Fairview Clinic began sending text reminders two days before each appointment.
sn.b: In March, the clinic also added evening appointment times on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
sn.c: The share of missed appointments fell from 18 percent in December to 9 percent in February.
sn.d: From March through May, the share of missed appointments stayed at about 9 percent.
sn.e: Patients who booked evening slots missed them less often than patients who booked morning slots.

R.w: Evening times began in March. Sentence 4 shows that the overall rate did not change after that point (about 9 percent from March through May), which directly supports the conclusion.

n.a: This gives the start date of the reminders. It says nothing about results after evening times were added.
n.b: This gives the start date of the evening times but no information about missed appointments afterward.
n.c: This drop happened before evening times existed. It suggests the reminders helped, but it does not show what happened after March.
n.e: This compares evening slots with morning slots. It does not show whether the clinic's overall rate changed, and at first glance it seems to point the other way.

R.q:
Read the notice.

Greenway Pharmacy Holiday Hours
Thanksgiving Day (Thursday, Nov. 27): Closed
Friday, Nov. 28: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Saturday, Nov. 29, and Sunday, Nov. 30: regular weekend hours, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Prescriptions due for refill between Nov. 26 and Nov. 28 may be picked up early, starting Monday, Nov. 24. Our drive-through window will open on Friday, Nov. 28, from 7 a.m. to 9 a.m. for prescription pickup; new prescriptions cannot be dropped off at the window. For urgent needs while we are closed, our 24-hour location at 410 Main Street will be open as usual.

Which statements are supported by the notice? Select all that apply.
o: The pharmacy's Main Street location will be open on Thanksgiving Day.
New prescriptions can be dropped off at the drive-through on Friday.
A prescription due for refill on Nov. 29 can be picked up on Nov. 24.
A prescription due for refill on Nov. 27 can be picked up on Nov. 24.
A customer can pick up a prescription at 8 a.m. on Friday, Nov. 28.
The pharmacy will stay open until 5 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 29.
R.w: The drive-through is open 7 to 9 a.m. on Nov. 28 for pickups. Refills due Nov. 26 to 28 (which includes Nov. 27) may be picked up starting Nov. 24. The 24-hour Main Street location stays open as usual while this store is closed.

n.1: The notice says new prescriptions cannot be dropped off at the window.
n.2: Early pickup applies to refills due Nov. 26 to Nov. 28, and Nov. 29 is outside that range.
n.5: Wrong row: 5 p.m. is Friday's closing time; Saturday hours end at 4 p.m.

R.q:
Rosa had worked weekend shifts at the hardware store since March, and every paycheck went into an envelope marked CAR. She had already turned down a beach trip in June and skipped the new phone that her friends all bought. By August, the envelope held $2,600 of the $3,000 her uncle was asking for his old sedan. On Friday, her friend Tasha called with news: she had two spare tickets to a concert in the city on Saturday, $150 each, and she wanted Rosa to come.

Based on the passage, how will Rosa most likely respond to Tasha's offer?
o: She will ask Tasha to lend her the money until her next paycheck arrives.
She will turn down the ticket so that she can keep saving for the car.
She will buy the ticket and ask her uncle to lower his price for the sedan.
She will accept the ticket because she has nearly reached her savings goal.
R.w: Rosa has repeatedly given up treats (a beach trip, a new phone) to save for the car and is still $400 short. Her established pattern points to declining the $150 ticket.

n.0: Borrowing from Tasha has no basis in the text and runs against her habit of saving every paycheck.
n.2: This needs an event the passage never suggests: nothing indicates the uncle would change his price.
n.3: Being close to the goal does not reverse her pattern; she is still $400 short, and nothing suggests she would stop saving now.

R.q:
Read the passage and the volunteer's list.

When a new book arrives at the Hillside Library, a technician first checks it against the order list to confirm it is the right title and edition. The book is then entered into the catalog, which assigns it a call number. Next, a label with the call number is attached to the spine, and a barcode is placed inside the front cover. The book is covered with a clear plastic jacket and stamped with the library's name. Finally, it is placed on the New Arrivals cart and shelved within two days.

Volunteer's list: (1) check against the order list; (2) enter into the catalog; (3) attach the spine label and barcode; (4) check out to the patron who requested it; (5) cover with a plastic jacket and stamp.

Which step in the volunteer's list is NOT part of the process described?
o: Step 3
Step 2
Step 4
Step 5
R.w: Checking a book out to a patron belongs to a different process (circulation). The passage's process ends with the book on the New Arrivals cart and shelved.

n.0: Attaching the spine label and barcode is the third step in the passage.
n.1: Entering the book into the catalog is the second step in the passage.
n.3: Covering and stamping the book is the fourth step in the passage.

R.q:
Read the passage.

In a growing number of counties, paramedics spend part of their shifts visiting patients at home rather than waiting for emergency calls. These community paramedicine programs focus on people who call 911 often or who were recently discharged from the hospital. During a visit, a paramedic may check blood pressure, review a patient's medicine bottles for duplicates, and look for hazards such as loose rugs. One county program reported that frequent callers enrolled for six months made about half as many 911 calls as before. Programs are often funded by grants, and some counties have struggled to keep them running when the grants end. Even so, supporters see home visits as a way to treat small problems before they become emergencies.

The main idea of the passage is that community paramedicine programs use home visits to head off emergencies. Which details from the passage support this main idea? Select all that apply.
o: Paramedics review patients' medicine bottles for duplicates.
Paramedics check patients' homes for hazards such as loose rugs.
Enrolled frequent callers made about half as many 911 calls.
Some counties have struggled to keep their programs running.
Paramedics visit patients in the hospital before discharge.
Programs are often paid for with grants that can run out.
R.w: A supporting detail shows how or that home visits prevent emergencies. Checking for duplicate medicines and for fall hazards are preventive actions, and the drop in 911 calls is evidence that the visits head off emergencies.

n.3: Struggling to keep programs running is a drawback the author concedes, not support for the main idea.
n.4: Distortion: the passage describes home visits to people already discharged, not hospital visits before discharge.
n.5: Grant funding is about how programs are paid for, a limitation rather than support for the idea that visits prevent emergencies.

R.q:
Every high school graduate in our state should leave knowing how to perform CPR. When a person's heart stops outside a hospital, the chance of survival drops with each minute before chest compressions begin, and many of these emergencies happen at home, in front of family members. Critics say schools already have too little time for core subjects. Yet hands-only CPR can be taught in a single 30-minute session, often during an existing health class. Several states already require the lesson, and none has reported that it crowded out other learning.

The sentence "Critics say schools already have too little time for core subjects" mainly serves to
o: concede that the author's proposal should wait until a later year
present an opposing view that the author then goes on to answer
give evidence that CPR training improves survival after cardiac arrest
state the main claim that the author supports throughout the passage
R.w: The sentence reports what critics say, and the next sentence begins "Yet" and answers it (the lesson takes one 30-minute session). It introduces a counterclaim that the author rebuts.

n.0: The author does not concede the point; the next sentence rejects it.
n.2: The survival evidence is in the second sentence; this sentence is about class time.
n.3: The main claim is the first sentence: every graduate should know CPR. This sentence presents a view that challenges it.

R.q:
The company claims its new wristband can detect dehydration before the wearer feels thirsty. Perhaps it can. But the company has not released any test data, and the two reviewers who wore the device during the same workout got readings that differed by 30 percent. Until an independent lab checks these claims, I would hold off on spending $199 for one. I'll believe it when I see the numbers.

Which word best describes the author's tone?
o: hostile
cynical
pessimistic
skeptical
R.w: The author doubts the claim but stays open to evidence ("Perhaps it can," "I'll believe it when I see the numbers"). Doubt that waits for proof is a skeptical tone.

n.0: "Hostile" suggests anger or attack; the author's language is measured and practical.
n.1: A cynical writer distrusts people's motives and assumes the worst. This author does not accuse the company of lying and allows that the device might work.
n.2: "Pessimistic" means expecting a bad outcome. The author withholds judgment until data arrive instead of predicting failure.

R.q:
Basic Sandwich Bread
1. Dissolve the yeast in water heated to between 105 and 115 °F. Water hotter than 130 °F kills yeast. Water cooler than 70 °F slows the yeast, so the dough rises much more slowly.
2. Stir in the flour, salt, and oil, and knead for 8 minutes.
3. Cover the bowl and let the dough rise until it has doubled in size, about 1 hour in a warm kitchen.
4. Shape the loaf and bake at 375 °F for 30 minutes.
Jamal follows every step but dissolves the yeast in tap water that is 60 °F.

Based on the recipe, what will most likely happen?
o: His dough will take longer than about an hour to double in size.
His dough will rise faster because cool water protects the yeast.
His dough will fail to rise because the cool water will kill the yeast.
His loaf will need less than 30 minutes of baking time to finish.
R.w: Step 1 says water cooler than 70 °F slows the yeast so the dough rises much more slowly. At 60 °F, Jamal's dough should take longer than the usual hour to double.

n.1: This reverses the recipe, which says cool water makes the dough rise more slowly.
n.2: The recipe says water hotter than 130 °F kills yeast; cool water slows it instead.
n.3: Nothing in the recipe links water temperature to baking time; this prediction has no support.

R.q:
A new study reports that adults who took VitaCore daily for 12 weeks had 30 percent fewer sick days than adults who took a placebo, or sugar pill. The study included 64 office workers in one city. It was paid for and run by VitaCore Nutrition, the company that sells the supplement, and its results have not been reviewed by outside scientists. VitaCore's website now calls the product "clinically proven to keep you healthy all year."

Which detail from the passage most strongly suggests that the study's findings may be biased?
o: The study compared the supplement with a placebo.
The study reported its main result as a percentage of sick days.
The study included 64 office workers from one city.
The supplement's seller paid for and ran the study.
R.w: A company that profits from the product has a financial interest in a favorable result. When the seller funds and runs its own study, the findings may be slanted toward the product, which is a classic source of bias.

n.0: A placebo comparison is a strength of study design; it helps rule out the effect of simply taking a pill.
n.1: Reporting a result as a percentage is a neutral way to present data and says nothing about whose interests the study serves.
n.2: A small, local sample makes the evidence less sufficient and harder to generalize, but that is a limitation of size, not a sign that the results were slanted toward one side.

R.q:
Dr. Nadia Hassan studied the X-ray for a long moment. She was almost sure the fracture would need surgery, but she wanted the orthopedic team to confirm it before she said anything to the family. In the waiting room, Mr. Brooks paced between the vending machine and the window, checking his phone every few seconds. His daughter sat with her arm in a sling, staring at the floor. When Dr. Hassan finally walked in, she smiled and said, "Let's talk about next steps."

Which point of view does the author use in the passage?
o: first person
third person omniscient
third person limited
third person objective
R.w: The narrator uses "she" and reports Dr. Hassan's private thoughts (she was almost sure about surgery, she wanted confirmation). Mr. Brooks and his daughter are shown only through their actions. Access to one character's mind is third person limited.

n.0: The narrator never says "I"; the only first-person words would be in dialogue, and there are none.
n.1: An omniscient narrator would reveal what Mr. Brooks and his daughter were thinking. Here we see only their actions.
n.3: An objective narrator reports only actions and speech, but this narrator tells us Dr. Hassan's thoughts.

R.q:
The Pine Lake reservoir supplies water to the town of Alder. The town's drought plan has three stages: Stage 1 (voluntary water conservation) begins when the reservoir falls below 70 percent of capacity, Stage 2 (lawn watering limited to two days a week) below 60 percent, and Stage 3 (no lawn watering) below 50 percent.
Date | Reservoir level
June 1 | 74%
July 1 | 68%
August 1 | 62%
Forecasters expect August to be as dry as July, and water use in town has stayed steady all summer.

If the pattern continues, which stage will most likely be in effect on September 1?
o: Stage 3, with lawn watering banned
Stage 2, with lawn watering two days a week
No stage, as rain refills the reservoir
Stage 1, with voluntary water conservation
R.w: Step 1: the level fell 6 points each month (74 to 68 to 62), and conditions are unchanged, so September 1 should be about 56 percent. Step 2: 56 percent is below 60 but above 50, which is Stage 2.

n.0: Stage 3 needs a level below 50 percent; at 6 points a month the reservoir should reach about 56 percent.
n.2: Forecasters expect another dry month and water use is steady, so nothing supports a reversal of the trend.
n.3: Stage 1 is the stage in effect on August 1 (62 percent); after another month of decline the level should drop below 60.

R.q:
Passage 1
Every Sunday, Abuela Rosa rolled tamales with her granddaughter Lucia, naming each step in Spanish. After Abuela died, Lucia found that she could still hear the words as her hands moved through the folding. Now she teaches the steps, in Spanish, to her own son.

Passage 2
My father kept his grandfather's fishing net long after the family boat was sold. When I asked why, he showed me how to mend it, knot by knot, the way his grandfather had shown him. I have never fished for a living, but I still mend nets each winter, and with each knot I picture my great-grandfather's hands at work.

Which themes are shared by both passages? Select all that apply.
o: Practical skills matter more than the money they can earn.
Language is the most important part of a family's heritage.
Repeating a family task can keep a loved one present in memory.
Children tend to reject the traditions their parents value.
Traditions passed down by hand keep a link to earlier generations.
Grief over a loss is eased by joining a new community.
R.w: In both, a hands-on skill (folding tamales, mending nets) is taught across generations, and doing it brings an ancestor to mind: Lucia hears Abuela's words, and the narrator pictures his great-grandfather's hands.

n.0: Passage 2 mentions not fishing for a living, but neither passage compares skills with money.
n.1: Language appears only in Passage 1, and neither passage ranks it as the most important part of heritage.
n.3: Both passages show children keeping traditions, the opposite of rejecting them.
n.5: Neither passage involves joining a new community; Lucia's comfort comes from a family practice.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Heat exhaustion occurs when the body loses too much water and salt, often through heavy sweating during hot weather or hard exercise. Its warning signs include heavy sweating, cool and clammy skin, muscle cramps, nausea, headache and dizziness. A person with heat exhaustion should move to a cooler place, loosen tight clothing and sip water. Heat stroke is more serious. It occurs when the body's temperature rises to 103 degrees Fahrenheit or higher, and the skin may become hot and red, either damp or dry. Heat stroke is an emergency: call 911 and cool the person right away.

According to the passage, which is a warning sign of heat stroke rather than heat exhaustion?
o: Muscle cramps along with nausea
A temperature of 103 degrees or higher
A headache with dizziness and nausea
Cool, clammy skin with heavy sweating
R.w: The passage describes heat stroke as occurring when body temperature reaches 103 degrees Fahrenheit or higher.

n.0: Muscle cramps and nausea are listed as signs of heat exhaustion.
n.2: Headache, dizziness and nausea are listed among the signs of heat exhaustion.
n.3: Cool, clammy skin and heavy sweating are listed as signs of heat exhaustion; heat stroke skin is described as hot and red.

R.q:
At a town meeting, the director of the Hillside Community Clinic said, "Our budget is $40,000 short this year. Either we close the clinic on Saturdays, or we raise the fee for every visit by $20. There is no other way to balance the books." Several residents pointed out that the clinic had not yet applied for a state grant, asked local businesses for support, or reviewed its supply costs.

Which fallacy does the director's statement contain?
o: Straw man
Slippery slope
Red herring
False dilemma
R.w: The director presents two options as the only choices, while residents name several others (a grant, business support, lower supply costs). Ignoring other options is a false dilemma.

n.0: A straw man misrepresents an opponent's position; the director does not describe anyone else's view.
n.1: A slippery slope predicts a chain of worsening events; the director predicts no chain.
n.2: A red herring switches to an unrelated topic; the director stays on the budget.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

A student is given this list of numbers: 12, 7, 18, 5, 9, 14. She carries out the steps below in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Remove every number less than 8.
2. Double each odd number that remains.
3. Arrange the numbers from greatest to least.
4. Add the first number in the list to the last number in the list.

What is the final result?
R.w: Step 1 removes 7 and 5: 12, 18, 9, 14. Step 2 doubles the only odd number, 9: 12, 18, 18, 14. Step 3: 18, 18, 14, 12. Step 4: 18 + 12 = 30.

n.0: Skips step 2, so 9 is never doubled: 18 + 9 = 27.
n.2: Adds the first number to the second-to-last number (18 + 14) instead of the last.
n.3: Doubles the odd numbers before removing small ones (applying step 2 to the original list), so 5 becomes 10 and stays: 18 + 10 = 28.

R.q: Read the passage. Select the sentence that best supports the claim made in the first sentence.

parts.t: Over the past two decades, the school nurse's job has shifted from treating playground injuries to managing students' ongoing health needs.
At Ridgeway Middle School, nurse Dana Price spends most mornings updating care plans with the families of students who have diabetes, asthma, or seizure disorders.
Each fall, she also checks every student's vision and hearing, a screening that school nurses have done for generations.
Scraped knees and bumped heads still arrive at her door, especially after recess.
Price says the hardest part of her job is keeping up with the paperwork that new state rules require.

sn.a: Over the past two decades, the school nurse's job has shifted from treating playground injuries to managing students' ongoing health needs.
sn.b: At Ridgeway Middle School, nurse Dana Price spends most mornings updating care plans with the families of students who have diabetes, asthma, or seizure disorders.
sn.c: Each fall, she also checks every student's vision and hearing, a screening that school nurses have done for generations.
sn.d: Scraped knees and bumped heads still arrive at her door, especially after recess.
sn.e: Price says the hardest part of her job is keeping up with the paperwork that new state rules require.

R.w: The claim is that the job now centers on managing ongoing health needs. Updating care plans for diabetes, asthma and seizure disorders is specific evidence of exactly that kind of ongoing management, so sentence 2 supports the claim most directly.

n.a: This is the claim itself. A sentence cannot serve as support for its own statement.
n.c: Vision and hearing screening goes beyond treating injuries, but the sentence itself says school nurses have done it for generations. It shows continuity in the job, not the shift toward managing ongoing health needs.
n.d: Scraped knees are the older kind of work the claim says the job has moved away from, so this detail does not support the shift.
n.e: This reports a complaint about paperwork. It does not show any change toward managing students' ongoing health needs.

R.q:
Read the passage.

The storm reached Port Allen just after midnight. While the wind tore shingles from roofs along the harbor, volunteers at the high school had already been setting up cots in the gym for two hours; they had begun at ten o'clock, right after the mayor ordered the evacuation of the low-lying east side. The power failed at 1:30 a.m., and the hospital switched to its backup generators within seconds. At dawn, the first rescue boats went out to the east side, where floodwater had reached the second step of many porches. By noon the water had begun to drop.

According to the passage, which event happened immediately before volunteers began setting up cots?
o: The power failed and the hospital started its generators.
The storm reached Port Allen just after midnight.
The wind tore shingles from roofs along the harbor.
The mayor ordered the evacuation of the east side.
R.w: Volunteers began at ten o'clock, "right after the mayor ordered the evacuation." The storm, the wind damage and the power failure all came later, after midnight.

n.0: The power failed at 1:30 a.m., long after the volunteers began at ten.
n.1: Order of mention trap: the storm is mentioned first but arrived after midnight, two hours after the cots were started.
n.2: The wind damage happened while the volunteers were already working, after midnight.

R.q:
Burns are grouped into types according to how deeply they damage the skin. A superficial burn, often called first-degree, affects only the outer layer of skin and causes redness and pain. A partial-thickness burn, or second-degree burn, reaches into the layer below and usually forms blisters. A full-thickness burn, or third-degree burn, destroys both layers and may look white, brown or leathery. Because nerve endings can be destroyed, a full-thickness burn may cause less pain than a smaller, shallower one.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: classification
chronological order
spatial order
cause and effect
R.w: The opening sentence says burns are "grouped into types," and the rest of the passage defines each type by its depth. Sorting a subject into categories is classification.

n.1: The types are listed by depth, not in time order; no events unfold.
n.2: Skin layers are mentioned, but the passage is not a description of where things are located in space; it defines categories.
n.3: The last sentence explains one cause and effect (destroyed nerves, less pain), but that detail sits inside the larger classification.

R.q:
Read the schedule.

Route 14 Weekday Schedule (all times a.m.)
Stop | Trip A | Trip B | Trip C | Trip D
Riverside Station | 6:30 | 6:55 | 7:20 | 7:45
Oak and 5th | 6:43 | 7:08 | 7:33 | 7:58
Mercy Hospital | 6:55 | 7:20 | 7:45 | 8:10
Lakeview College | 7:07 | 7:32 | 7:57 | 8:22
Saturday service: Trips B and D run at the times shown. Trips A and C do not run on Saturdays.

Tomas must arrive at Mercy Hospital by 8:00 a.m. on a Saturday. He will board the bus at Oak and 5th. What is the latest departure he can take from that stop?
R.w: On Saturdays, only Trips B and D run. Trip D reaches Mercy Hospital at 8:10, too late. Trip B leaves Oak and 5th at 7:08 and reaches the hospital at 7:20.

n.0: 7:20 is Trip B's arrival time at Mercy Hospital, or Trip C's departure from Riverside Station, not a departure from Oak and 5th that fits.
n.1: Trip D leaves Oak and 5th at 7:58 but does not reach the hospital until 8:10.
n.3: Trip C would work on a weekday, but it does not run on Saturdays.

R.q:
Read the label.

Nutrition Facts
Servings per container: 3
Serving size: 1 cup (240 mL)
Amount per serving
Calories: 150
Total Fat: 4 g (5% Daily Value)
Sodium: 480 mg (21% Daily Value)
Total Carbohydrate: 22 g (8% Daily Value)
   Dietary Fiber: 5 g (18% Daily Value)
   Total Sugars: 6 g
Protein: 7 g
Ingredients: water, black beans, tomatoes, onions, corn, salt, chili powder, garlic.

Keisha heats the soup and eats two servings. Based on the label, how much sodium does she consume?
o: 42 mg
480 mg
960 mg
R.w: Label amounts are per serving. Keisha eats 2 servings, so 2 x 480 mg = 960 mg of sodium.

n.0: Doubles the 21% Daily Value and treats the 42 as milligrams.
n.1: 480 mg is the amount in one serving, but Keisha eats two.
n.3: 1,440 mg is the sodium in the whole container (3 servings), not in the 2 servings she eats.

R.q:
The Millbrook City Council voted 5 to 2 in June to spend $1.2 million on the River Walk Trail. Construction crews began clearing the route along the riverbank in August. When finished, the paved trail will be 3.4 miles long, according to the approved plans. Council member Dana Whitfield, who voted yes, told reporters, "This trail will draw thousands of new visitors and bring our downtown shops back to life."

Which of the following statements from the article is an opinion?
o: The trail will draw thousands of new visitors and revive downtown shops.
The approved plans call for a paved trail 3.4 miles long.
Construction crews began clearing the route along the riverbank in August.
The council voted 5 to 2 in June to spend $1.2 million on the River Walk Trail.
R.w: Whitfield is predicting future results and judging their effect on downtown. A prediction like this cannot be proven when it is made, and others may expect different results, so it is an opinion.

n.1: The planned length is written in the approved documents and can be checked now, so this is a fact about the plan, not a guess about the future.
n.2: The start of construction can be confirmed by records or observation, so this is a fact.
n.3: The vote count and amount are part of the public council record, so they are facts.

R.q:
Email from Dana Price: The CPR instructor training starts at 9:00 a.m. on Thursday at the County Health Building on Fifth Street. Please arrive 15 minutes early to sign in and pick up your materials. The building is a 10-minute walk from the Fifth Street bus stop.

Route 12 weekday schedule, arrival times at Fifth Street
7:52 a.m. | 8:22 a.m. | 8:37 a.m. | 8:52 a.m. | 9:07 a.m.

Omar is taking Route 12 to the training. Based on the email and the schedule, which is the latest bus he can take and still arrive in time to sign in?
o: The 8:52 a.m. bus
The 8:37 a.m. bus
The 7:52 a.m. bus
The 8:22 a.m. bus
R.w: Step 1: arriving 15 minutes before 9:00 means being at the building by 8:45. Step 2: with a 10-minute walk, the bus must reach Fifth Street by 8:35. The latest bus that does is the 8:22.

n.0: The 8:52 bus plus the walk arrives at 9:02, which misses sign-in and is late for the start.
n.1: The 8:37 bus plus a 10-minute walk reaches the building at 8:47, after the 8:45 sign-in time.
n.2: The 7:52 bus works, but the question asks for the latest bus that still gets him there in time.

R.q:
Until this spring, residents of Carver County who needed mental health support after business hours had to call a regional hotline based two states away or go to an emergency room. Launched in April, the county's new 24-hour crisis line answered 3,800 calls in its first six months, and it is an overdue improvement for families who once waited days for help. The line is staffed by licensed counselors and costs callers nothing.

In the second sentence, which word or phrase makes the sentence a statement of opinion?
o: answered 3,800 calls
overdue
24-hour
new
R.w: "Overdue" judges that the service should have existed sooner. That is a value judgment others may not share, so it turns the sentence into an opinion. The other details can all be checked.

n.0: A call count can be confirmed from the line's records. A number inside a sentence does not decide whether the sentence is a fact or an opinion.
n.2: The line's hours of operation can be verified, so "24-hour" is factual.
n.3: "New" can be checked against the April launch date, so here it states a fact rather than a judgment.

R.q:
Read the instructions.

Patient Registration Form: Instructions
Section A: All patients complete.
Section B: Complete if you have health insurance. If you are covered by more than one plan, list the primary plan first.
Section C: Complete if the patient is under 18; a parent or legal guardian must sign.
Section D: Complete if you are applying for the clinic's sliding-fee discount. Attach a recent pay stub or tax return.
Section E: All patients sign and date.

Luis is 34 years old. He has no health insurance, and he is applying for the clinic's sliding-fee discount.

Which sections should Luis complete?
o: Sections A, D and E
Sections A and E, and attach a pay stub
Sections A, B, D and E
Sections A, C, D and E
R.w: Every patient completes A and E. Section D applies because Luis is applying for the discount. Section B applies to insured patients and Section C to patients under 18, and neither describes Luis.

n.1: The pay stub goes with Section D, which Luis must also complete.
n.2: Section B is for patients with insurance, and Luis has none.
n.3: Section C is for patients under 18, and Luis is 34.

R.q:
Report A, from the state health department: 48 percent of adults in the state get regular exercise, defined as at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week.

Report B, from a fitness company: 72 percent of adults in the state exercise regularly, defined as working out at least once a week for any length of time.

Both reports surveyed randomly selected adults in the same state during the same year, and both asked about exercise over the past month.

Which statement best explains the difference between the two reports' findings?
o: Report B's definition of regular exercise is easier to meet.
Report A counted adults over age 65 and left out younger adults.
The fitness company rounded its figure up to the nearest ten.
Report B surveyed adults in a different year than Report A did.
R.w: Report A requires 150 minutes a week; Report B counts anyone who works out once a week for any length of time. A looser definition counts more people, which explains the higher percentage.

n.1: Nothing in the passage limits Report A to older adults; it describes adults in the state.
n.2: 72 is not a multiple of ten, so it was not rounded to the nearest ten, and rounding could not explain a 24-point gap.
n.3: The passage says both reports surveyed adults in the same year.

R.q:
Why do so many water mains break in January? Water expands by about 9 percent when it freezes. When the ground around a buried pipe freezes, it shifts and pushes against the pipe, placing stress on joints and older sections. Cold water inside the pipe also makes metal and plastic more brittle. As a result, a pipe that has handled years of normal pressure can crack during a hard freeze. Older cast-iron mains are especially likely to fail because decades of corrosion have already thinned their walls.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: problem and solution
chronological order
classification
cause and effect
R.w: The passage opens with a "why" question and answers it with causes (freezing, shifting ground, brittleness, corrosion) and their effect (cracked pipes). Signal words such as "as a result" and "because" confirm a cause-and-effect structure.

n.0: The passage explains the breaks but proposes no fix, so it lacks the solution half of this structure.
n.1: The passage explains why something happens, not a series of events in time order.
n.2: Cast-iron mains are singled out once, but the passage does not sort pipes into categories.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a rural clinic director: Since we began offering video visits, patients who once drove ninety minutes for a five-minute medication check can now do it from home. Video works well for follow-ups. Some problems, such as a new lump or chest pain, still require an in-person exam.

Passage 2
From a patient advocate: Telehealth is convenient for many patients, but many older adults in our county lack reliable internet. Insurers should pay for phone-only visits as well as video. Even then, telehealth should add to the clinic, not replace it.

Which statements would both authors most likely agree with? Select all that apply.
o: Follow-up visits work best when they are done by video.
Telehealth makes care more convenient for many patients.
Rural patients are the main users of telehealth services.
Insurers should pay for phone-only visits as well as video.
Most older adults in the county lack internet at home.
Telehealth cannot take the place of every in-person visit.
R.w: The director praises saved drives and the advocate calls telehealth convenient for many. The director says some problems need an in-person exam, and the advocate says telehealth should add to the clinic, not replace it.

n.0: The director says video works well for follow-ups; the advocate does not comment on follow-ups.
n.2: Neither passage compares rural patients with other users.
n.3: Only the advocate calls for phone-only coverage; the director does not address insurance.
n.4: The advocate says many older adults lack reliable internet, not most, and the director does not discuss it.

R.q:
Read the label.

Drug Facts
Active ingredient (in each tablet): Ibuprofen 200 mg. Purpose: pain reliever and fever reducer.
Uses: temporarily relieves minor aches and pains due to headache, toothache, backache, menstrual cramps, the common cold and muscle aches; temporarily reduces fever.
Directions: Adults and children 12 years and over: take 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours while symptoms last. If pain or fever does not respond to 1 tablet, 2 tablets may be used. Do not take more than 6 tablets in 24 hours unless a doctor directs you to. Children under 12: ask a doctor.
Stop use and ask a doctor if: pain gets worse or lasts more than 10 days; fever gets worse or lasts more than 3 days.

According to the label, when should an adult stop using the product and ask a doctor?
o: When more than 2 tablets are needed in a day
When a fever has lasted for more than 3 days
When one tablet does not relieve the pain
When pain has lasted for more than 3 days
R.w: The "Stop use and ask a doctor if" section lists a fever that gets worse or lasts more than 3 days.

n.0: The daily limit is 6 tablets in 24 hours, so needing more than 2 is within the directions.
n.2: If 1 tablet does not work, the directions allow 2 tablets; this is not a reason to stop.
n.3: Mixes up the limits: the label allows pain to last up to 10 days before asking a doctor; 3 days is the fever limit.

R.q:
Read the passage.

A first-time blood donor often expects the process to take a few minutes, but a whole visit usually lasts about an hour. It begins with registration, where the donor shows identification and reads information about who should not give blood.

Next comes a brief health screening in a private area. A staff member checks the donor's temperature, pulse and blood pressure and pricks a finger to make sure the donor's iron level is high enough. Only then does the donation itself begin, and it takes roughly ten minutes to collect about a pint.

Afterward, donors rest for about fifteen minutes and have a snack and a drink, which helps prevent dizziness before they leave.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Staff check each donor's temperature, pulse, blood pressure and iron level before the donation starts.
The donation itself takes about ten minutes and collects roughly one pint of blood from the donor.
Most first-time donors feel dizzy after giving blood, so they must rest and eat before they leave.
Giving blood takes about an hour: registration, a health screening, a short donation and a brief rest.
R.w: The passage states that a visit lasts about an hour and then walks through its stages in order: registration, screening, donation and rest. This option captures the main point and every stage in sequence.

n.0: Too narrow: the screening checks are details of a single stage.
n.1: Too narrow: the length of the draw is one detail from the second paragraph.
n.2: Distortion: the rest and snack help prevent dizziness; the passage never says most donors feel dizzy.

R.q:
Starting next month, Summit Medical Group will ask patients to complete their check-in forms online before they arrive. Patients who arrive without completing the form can fill it out on a tablet in the waiting room, which takes about 10 minutes. During a three-month pilot at one office, average check-in time at the front desk fell from 7 minutes to 2 minutes for patients who completed the form at home. About a third of the patients in the pilot arrived without completing it.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage?
o: Summit will remove the waiting-room tablets after next month because few patients use them.
Many patients will stop booking appointments with Summit because of the new form.
Patients who skip the online form will likely take longer to check in than those who complete it.
Average check-in time at each Summit office will likely fall to about 2 minutes per patient.
R.w: Patients who completed the form at home checked in in about 2 minutes, while those who arrive without it need about 10 minutes on a tablet. The passage supports a longer check-in for patients who skip the form.

n.0: About a third of pilot patients needed the tablet, so the passage suggests the tablets will be used, not removed.
n.1: Nothing in the passage suggests patients will leave; this prediction has no support.
n.3: Two minutes applied to patients who completed the form; with about a third arriving without it, the overall average would be higher.

R.q:
Coach Rivera paced the sideline, certain that his team had one more good play left in them. On the bench, Tyler rubbed his sore ankle and hoped the coach would not notice, because he wanted desperately to finish the game. In the stands, Tyler's mother gripped her program and wondered whether she should have let him play at all. And the referee, who had made a questionable call in the first half, quietly promised himself that he would get the next one right.

Which point of view does the author use?
o: third person objective
first person, told by an observer
third person limited
third person omniscient
R.w: The narrator stands outside the story and reveals the private thoughts of four different people: the coach, Tyler, his mother and the referee. Knowing the minds of many characters is third person omniscient.

n.0: An objective narrator reports only what can be seen and heard, but this narrator tells us what each person hopes, wonders and promises privately.
n.1: No narrator refers to himself or herself as "I," not even an onlooker; every character is described from outside.
n.2: A limited narrator reveals one character's thoughts; this one moves freely among several.

R.q:
Andre has just been assigned a group project on sickle cell disease, a topic he knows little about. Before he reads the detailed research articles his group has collected, he wants a short, reliable overview of what the disease is, how it is inherited, and its main symptoms, so that he can follow the technical terms in those articles. His group meets on Thursday to divide up the reading.

Which source would best serve Andre's purpose?
o: A patient's blog about daily life with sickle cell disease
A current medical encyclopedia entry on sickle cell disease
An article reporting a new gene therapy trial in 40 patients
A news story about a fundraising walk for sickle cell research
R.w: A current encyclopedia entry is a tertiary source designed to give a broad, reliable overview of a topic, which is exactly what Andre needs before reading detailed research.

n.0: A personal blog gives one person's experience, not a reliable overview of the disease.
n.2: A single trial report is primary research on one narrow question and assumes the background Andre lacks.
n.3: A story about a fundraiser does not explain the disease, its inheritance, or symptoms.

R.q:
Marcus signed up to volunteer at Maple Court Senior Living because his school required twenty service hours. For the first few Thursdays, he read the newspaper aloud to Mr. Hale, who corrected his pronunciation and rarely smiled. Marcus counted the minutes. In October, Mr. Hale mentioned that he had once flown cargo planes in Alaska. Curious, Marcus asked a question, and then another. By December, Marcus had logged sixty hours, far more than he needed, and had filled a notebook with Mr. Hale's stories.

Which statement expresses a theme of the passage rather than its topic or plot?
o: A high school student's volunteer work at a senior living center
Marcus logs sixty hours after he begins asking Mr. Hale about Alaska.
Schools should require students to complete community service hours.
Curiosity about others can turn an obligation into a real connection.
R.w: A theme is a general message stated as a full sentence. Marcus's attitude changes when he becomes curious about Mr. Hale, turning required hours into a relationship he values.

n.0: This phrase names the topic; it states no message.
n.1: This retells events from the plot rather than stating a general message.
n.2: This is an opinion about school policy; the story never argues for requiring service hours.

R.q:
After her knee replacement, Mrs. Tran was ambulatory by the second day; that is, she could make it to the end of the hallway and back with a cane for support. The physical therapist recorded her distance each afternoon and expected her to manage the stairs before the end of the week.

As used in the passage, the word ambulatory most nearly means
o: free of pain.
in need of an ambulance.
ready to go home.
able to walk.
R.w: The phrase "that is" introduces a restatement: she could make it down the hallway and back with a cane. Ambulatory means able to walk.

n.0: The passage says nothing about pain; walking with a cane does not tell us whether she still hurts.
n.1: "Ambulance" looks and sounds similar, but the passage describes her moving on her own, not being transported.
n.2: Discharge is not mentioned, and the therapist still expects more progress this week, so "ready to go home" goes beyond the clue.

R.q:
The blue light from phones and tablets signals the brain to stay awake, and a 2023 survey found that children who used screens in the hour before bed slept 40 minutes less on school nights than children who did not. Tired children struggle to pay attention in class and are more likely to be irritable. Parents, it is time to act. Set a family rule that all screens go into a basket in the kitchen one hour before bedtime, and follow the rule yourselves.

Which of the following best states the author's purpose?
o: to discuss the topic of children's sleep and electronic devices
to report the results of a 2023 survey about children's screen use
to describe a typical bedtime routine in an American family
to convince parents to limit children's screen use before bed
R.w: The passage builds to direct commands ("Parents, it is time to act. Set a family rule..."), so its purpose is to convince parents to take a specific action.

n.0: This names the topic, not the purpose. It leaves out the author's clear push for a particular action.
n.1: The survey is one piece of supporting evidence; the passage does not report its methods or full results.
n.2: The basket in the kitchen is a recommendation, not a description of what families already do.

R.q:
Timeline: Harbor Street Clinic
1998 | Clinic opens with two exam rooms
2004 | Dental services added
2011 | Clinic moves to a larger building on Pier Avenue
2016 | Evening hours begin
2021 | Telehealth visits begin

From the clinic's anniversary newsletter: The year after the clinic moved, it hired its first full-time Spanish interpreter. Two years after hiring the interpreter, it started a diabetes education class. The class became so popular that a second weekly session was added in the same year that evening hours began.

Based on the timeline and the newsletter, in what year did the diabetes education class start?
R.w: Step 1: the clinic moved in 2011 (timeline), so the interpreter was hired in 2012. Step 2: the class started two years after the hire, in 2014.

n.0: 2016 is when evening hours began and the second session was added, not when the class started.
n.1: 2013 counts two years from the move (2011) instead of from the interpreter's hiring (2012).
n.2: 2012 is the year the interpreter was hired, one step early.

R.q:
Our county should require bicycle helmets for riders under 16. Head injuries are the leading cause of serious harm in bicycle crashes, and a helmet that fits correctly greatly lowers the risk of a brain injury. In the past three years, the county trauma center treated 46 children for head injuries from bike crashes, and only 5 of them had been wearing helmets. Helmets now cost as little as $15, and the fire department gives them away free at every spring safety fair. A helmet rule would protect our children at little cost to families.

Which element of a complete argument is missing from the passage?
o: A clear claim that the author wants readers to accept
A reason explaining why the claim deserves support
A response to an objection that opponents might raise
Evidence that supports the reasons behind the claim
R.w: The passage states a claim, gives reasons (head injuries, low cost), and supports them with evidence (46 children, 5 in helmets; $15 helmets). It never raises or answers an opposing view, such as concerns about enforcement or personal choice.

n.0: The first sentence states the claim directly: require helmets for riders under 16.
n.1: The passage gives reasons: helmets lower brain injury risk and cost families little.
n.3: The trauma center figures and the helmet prices are evidence.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Start with the word HOSPITAL. Carry out the steps below in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Remove the second letter.
2. Replace every vowel (A, E, I, O, U) with the letter that comes immediately after it in the alphabet.
3. Move the last letter to the front of the word.
4. Reverse the order of all the letters.
5. Insert the letter R between the third and fourth letters.

Which of the following is the final result?
o: BTJRPSHL
BTRJPSHL
BTJPSHL
LBTRJPSH
R.w: HOSPITAL, step 1: HSPITAL. Step 2 (I to J, A to B): HSPJTBL. Step 3: LHSPJTB. Step 4: BTJPSHL. Step 5, R between the third letter (J) and the fourth (P): BTJRPSHL.

n.1: Off by one: the R was placed between the second and third letters.
n.2: This is the result after step 4; step 5's inserted R is missing.
n.3: Step 3 was skipped: reversing HSPJTBL gives LBTJPSH, and inserting R gives LBTRJPSH.

R.q:
Read the handbook section.

Volunteer Handbook, Section 4: Patient Escort
As you practiced during orientation, lock both wheels of a wheelchair before a patient sits down or stands up. Use the service elevators near the cafeteria rather than the public elevators in the main lobby, which are often crowded during visiting hours. Volunteers do not move patients on stretchers or patients connected to IV pumps; ask the unit clerk to page transport staff instead. If a patient says they feel faint, stop, lock the wheels and call for help using the nearest staff phone.

Which assumption about its readers does the handbook's author most clearly make?
o: Readers have worked as transport staff at other hospitals.
Readers know how to operate IV pumps safely on their own.
Readers have already attended an orientation session.
Readers usually work their shifts during visiting hours.
R.w: The phrase "As you practiced during orientation" shows the author expects readers to have attended orientation already.

n.0: Unsupported: readers are told to ask for transport staff, which suggests they are not transport staff.
n.1: Contradicted: volunteers are told not to move patients connected to IV pumps.
n.3: Unsupported: visiting hours are mentioned only to explain why the lobby elevators are crowded.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Grandpa Eli unfolded the paper map across the hood of the station wagon and traced the route with his finger. The nearest pay phone was back at the gas station, eleven miles behind them, and the last town had been too small for a motel. Ruthie, nine years old, rewound the tape in her cassette player with a pencil because the batteries had died somewhere in Nebraska. Her mother checked the cooler: four sandwiches, a jar of pickles and two warm sodas. "We'll make Cheyenne by dark," Grandpa said, though no one had seen a road sign in nearly an hour.

Based on details in the passage, when does the story most likely take place?
o: During the early years of the automobile, in the first decade of the 1900s
In a time before cell phones and digital music players were common
In the present day, on a road with no cell phone coverage
In midwinter, when snow often closes the roads in Nebraska
R.w: A paper map, a pay phone eleven miles back and a battery-powered cassette player point to a time after cassettes were common but before cell phones and digital music were. The family relies on a pay phone, not a phone they carry.

n.0: Cassette players and station wagons rule out the first decade of the 1900s.
n.2: A cassette player and a pay phone as the nearest phone point to the past, not the present day.
n.3: Nothing mentions snow or cold; the warm sodas, if anything, suggest the opposite.

R.q:
Read the passage.

A city health report found that neighborhoods with more fast-food restaurants per block also had higher rates of diabetes. The same neighborhoods had fewer full-service grocery stores, lower average incomes and fewer parks than other parts of the city. The report's authors noted that their data showed only where these features occurred together, not which ones, if any, caused the others. They recommended a follow-up study that would track the same residents over several years.

Which statement is best supported by the report as described?
o: Residents of these neighborhoods prefer fast food to meals that they cook at home.
Closing fast-food restaurants would lower the city's rate of diabetes.
Diabetes is more common where several features cluster, but the cause is unclear.
Fast-food restaurants are the main cause of diabetes in these neighborhoods.
R.w: The report found that several features (fast food, fewer groceries, lower incomes, fewer parks) occur together with higher diabetes rates, and the authors state that the data do not show cause. This option keeps to that limit.

n.0: Unsupported: the report describes restaurant counts, not what residents prefer to eat.
n.1: A prediction that assumes fast food causes diabetes, which the data do not show.
n.3: Treats a correlation as a cause, which the authors explicitly warn against.

R.q:
Passage 1
City council member Ortiz: Painted bike lanes do little when a delivery truck can park in them. Protected lanes, separated from traffic by curbs or posts, are the surest way to make cycling safe enough that families will try it. The city should build them on its three busiest streets.

Passage 2
City council member Bennett: Protected lanes cost about ten times as much per mile as paint. For the same money, we could add painted lanes across the city and lower the downtown speed limit to 20 miles per hour, which would protect cyclists on every street, not just three.

Which assumption do both council members share?
o: The city's budget cannot pay for any protected bike lanes.
Lower speed limits would reduce car traffic in the downtown area.
Protected lanes are the best choice for keeping cyclists safe.
Making streets safer for cyclists is a worthwhile goal for the city.
R.w: Ortiz and Bennett differ on the method, but both propose spending to protect cyclists. Neither questions the goal itself, so it is the assumption they share.

n.0: Bennett says protected lanes cost more, not that the city cannot afford any.
n.1: Bennett proposes lower speeds to protect cyclists, not to reduce traffic, and Ortiz does not mention speed.
n.2: This is Ortiz's position; Bennett argues that paint plus lower speeds would protect more cyclists.

R.q:
The storm had knocked out the power for the third time that afternoon. Water was dripping from a crack in the kitchen ceiling into a row of mixing bowls, the basement was flooding, and the phone battery was at four percent. Marcus looked around the dark, damp room, sighed, and said to his sister, "Well, this is turning out to be a relaxing weekend."

Marcus's statement is an example of which of the following?
o: hyperbole
verbal irony
personification
situational irony
R.w: Marcus says the weekend is "relaxing" when he means the opposite. Saying one thing while meaning its opposite is verbal irony.

n.0: Hyperbole exaggerates the truth; Marcus reverses the truth rather than overstating it.
n.2: Marcus gives no human traits to an object; he comments on his own weekend.
n.3: Situational irony is an outcome that is the opposite of what is expected. The storm is unfortunate, but the irony here lies in Marcus's words, not in an unexpected outcome.

R.q:
(1) Every year, the Ridgeview public pool opens on Memorial Day and closes on Labor Day. (2) Yet the hottest weeks in our town now often arrive in September, when the pool sits empty behind a locked gate. (3) Ridgeview should keep the pool open through the end of September. (4) Last year, the high temperature topped 90 °F on eleven September days. (5) Some council members worry about the cost of lifeguards once college students return to school. (6) But the high school swim team has offered certified lifeguards on weekends, and extra admission fees would cover weekday staff.

Which sentence states the author's main claim?
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
Sentence 6
R.w: Sentence 3 states the position the whole letter defends: keep the pool open through September. The other sentences give reasons, evidence, an objection, and a response to it.

n.1: Sentence 2 is a reason for the claim (the hot weeks have shifted), not the position itself.
n.2: Sentence 4 is evidence, a statistic supporting the reason in Sentence 2.
n.3: Sentence 6 is a rebuttal that answers the cost objection raised in Sentence 5.

R.q:
Read the description of the flowchart.

Flowchart: Front Desk Check-In
Start: "Does the patient have an appointment today?"
If NO, go to: "Is the patient having chest pain or trouble breathing?" If YES: "Send to the emergency department." If NO: "Offer the next walk-in slot."
If YES, go to: "Is the patient more than 15 minutes late?" If YES: "Offer to reschedule the appointment." If NO: "Verify insurance," then "Send to the waiting room."

A patient who has an appointment arrives 20 minutes late. She has no chest pain or trouble breathing. According to the flowchart, what should the receptionist do?
o: Offer her the next available walk-in slot
Send her to the emergency department
Offer to reschedule her appointment
Verify her insurance and send her to the waiting room
R.w: She has an appointment, so follow the YES branch to the lateness question. She is 20 minutes late, which is more than 15, so the chart says to offer to reschedule.

n.0: The walk-in slot is on the branch for patients without an appointment.
n.1: The emergency department branch is for patients without an appointment who have chest pain or trouble breathing.
n.3: This is the path for a patient who is 15 minutes late or less.

M.q: A clinic buys 38 boxes of syringes at $19.75 per box. Rounding each number to the nearest ten, which is the estimate of the total cost?
M.w: 38 rounds to 40 and $19.75 rounds to $20. Estimate: 40 × $20 = $800. (The exact cost is $750.50.)

n.0: $400 rounds $19.75 down to $10; the ones digit 9 means rounding up to $20.
n.1: $300 truncates both numbers (30 × $10) instead of rounding.
n.2: $600 rounds 38 down to 30; the ones digit 8 means rounding up to 40.

M.q: A storage room is 4 yards long, 3 yards wide, and 3 yards high. A ventilation fan is sized by the number of cubic feet of air in the room. What is the volume of the room in cubic feet?
o: 36 ft³
108 ft³
324 ft³
972 ft³
M.w: V = 4 × 3 × 3 = 36 yd³. 36 × 27 = 972 ft³. (Or convert first: 12 ft × 9 ft × 9 ft = 972 ft³.)

n.0: 36 is the volume in cubic yards, not cubic feet.
n.1: This multiplies 36 yd³ by 3; 1 yd³ = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 ft³.
n.2: This multiplies 36 yd³ by 9, which is the square-yard factor.

M.q: A medication is ordered at 15 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, divided into 3 equal doses. A child weighs 44 pounds. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milligrams should be given in each dose?
o: 300 mg
100 mg
660 mg
220 mg
M.w: Weight: 44 ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg. Daily dose: 15 × 20 = 300 mg. Each dose: 300 ÷ 3 = 100 mg.

n.0: This is the total daily dose; it must be divided into 3 equal doses.
n.2: This uses the weight in pounds and also gives a daily total, 44 × 15.
n.3: This uses the weight in pounds (44 × 15 ÷ 3) instead of converting to 20 kg first.

M.q: For a clinic open house, each of 5 tables needs 3 quarts of lemonade. The lemonade is sold in half-gallon jugs. What is the least number of jugs that must be bought to supply all 5 tables?
M.w: Total = 5 × 3 = 15 qt. A gallon is 4 qt, so a half gallon is 2 qt. 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5, so round up to 8 jugs.

n.0: This divides by 4 quarts, the amount in a full gallon rather than a half gallon.
n.2: This multiplies 15 quarts by 2 instead of dividing by the 2 quarts in each jug.
n.3: 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5, and 7 jugs hold 14 qt, which is not enough, so round up.

M.q: A patient's oral temperature is recorded as 38.5 °C in the hospital chart. The patient's home thermometer reads in degrees Fahrenheit. What is the patient's temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?

n.1: This rounds 38.5 °C up to 39 °C before converting; round only at the end, and (9/5)(38.5) + 32 = 101.3 °F.
n.2: This adds the 1.5 °C above normal (37 °C) to 98.6 °F. Each Celsius degree equals 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees, so the reading is 2.7 °F above normal.
n.3: This multiplies by 2 instead of 9/5 (2 × 38.5 + 32 = 109); the factor is 9/5 = 1.8.

M.q: A square bulletin board covers 196 square inches of wall space. A teacher wants to staple decorative trim around its entire edge. How many inches of trim are needed?
o: 56 in
98 in
14 in
49 in
M.w: Side = square root of 196 = 14 in, because 14 × 14 = 196. Perimeter = 4 × 14 = 56 in.

n.1: This divides the area by 2 instead of finding the side length.
n.2: 14 in is the length of one side, not the distance around the board.
n.3: This divides the area by 4; find the side length first (the square root of 196 is 14 in).

M.q: A child's dose of a liquid medicine, M, in milliliters, is calculated from the child's weight, W, in kilograms, using the formula M = 0.4W. Which statement is correct?
o: M is independent, because the dose is what the nurse controls
M is independent, and W rises by 2 kg when M rises by 5 mL
W is independent, and M rises by 12.5 mL when W rises by 5 kg
W is independent, and M rises by 2 mL when W rises by 5 kg
M.w: The dose is calculated from the weight, so W is independent and M is dependent. An increase of 5 kg changes M by 0.4 x 5 = 2 mL.

n.0: The dose is the output of the formula; the weight is the input.
n.1: This swaps the variables; the dose is calculated from the weight.
n.2: 5 / 0.4 = 12.5 divides by the rate instead of multiplying: 0.4 x 5 = 2 mL.

M.q: A circular pool with a radius of 9 feet is surrounded by a concrete walkway 3 feet wide. A fence will be built along the outer edge of the walkway. How long will the fence be? Use 3.14 for pi.
M.w: Outer radius = 9 + 3 = 12 ft. C = 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 12 = 75.36 ft.

n.0: This is the area inside the fence (3.14 × 12²), not its length.
n.2: This uses the pool's radius (9 ft); the fence is at the outer edge, 12 ft from the center.
n.3: This adds the 3-foot walkway to the diameter once (21 ft); it adds 3 ft on each side (24 ft).

M.q: A histogram shows the birth weights of 40 infants: 5.0-5.9 lb, 3 infants; 6.0-6.9 lb, 9 infants; 7.0-7.9 lb, 15 infants; 8.0-8.9 lb, 10 infants; 9.0-9.9 lb, 3 infants. Which statement is supported by the histogram?
o: More than one-third of the infants weighed 8.0 pounds or more
Fewer than 1 in 3 infants weighed under 7.0 pounds
Exactly 15 infants weighed 7.5 pounds
The heaviest infant weighed 9.9 pounds
M.w: Under 7.0 lb: 3 + 9 = 12 infants. 12 / 40 = 30%, which is less than 1/3 (about 33.3%).

n.0: 10 + 3 = 13 infants, and 13 / 40 = 32.5%, which is less than one-third (33.3%).
n.2: The 15 infants weighed somewhere from 7.0 to 7.9 lb; a histogram does not give single values.
n.3: The top interval shows only that the heaviest infants weighed between 9.0 and 9.9 lb.

M.q: A patient weighed 187 pounds at admission and 176 pounds at discharge. The chart records weight in kilograms. Use 1 kilogram = 2.2 pounds. How many kilograms did the patient lose during the hospital stay?
o: 11 kg
5 kg
85 kg

n.0: This multiplies the 11 lb loss by 2.2; pounds to kilograms means dividing by 2.2.
n.1: 11 is the loss in pounds; it still has to be divided by 2.2.
n.3: 85 kg is the admission weight (187 ÷ 2.2), not the amount lost.

M.q: A uniform store lists the original price, the discount and the sale price of six items. Select the sale price that was calculated incorrectly.
M.w: Sale price = price x (1 - discount rate). Shoes: 120 x 0.85 = $102.00. The listed $105.00 subtracts 15 dollars instead of 15 percent (15% of $120 is $18).

n.a: 40 x 0.75 = 30.00, so this sale price is correct.
n.b: 85 x 0.80 = 68.00, so this sale price is correct.
n.d: 36 x 0.70 = 25.20, so this sale price is correct.
n.e: 12.50 x 0.60 = 7.50, so this sale price is correct.
n.f: 64 x 0.65 = 41.60, so this sale price is correct. (The discount itself is 64 x 0.35 = $22.40.)

M.q: A number line runs from 0 to 2, with tick marks every 1/4 unit starting at 0. Point A is on the 7th tick mark to the right of 0. What is the value of point A?
M.w: Each tick is 1/4 unit, so 7 ticks to the right of 0 is 7 × 1/4 = 7/4 = 1 3/4.

n.0: 7/8 treats each tick as 1/8, as if the 8 intervals covered 0 to 1 instead of 0 to 2.
n.1: 1 1/2 = 6/4 counts the tick at 0 as the first tick mark.
n.3: 1.7 treats each tick as 0.1; the ticks are quarters, not tenths.

M.q: A pharmacy charges a monthly delivery fee of $12 plus $1.75 for each delivery. A patient's statement shows $54 in delivery charges for the month. How many deliveries did the patient receive? Enter the number of deliveries.

tr.42: Subtracted the $12 fee but did not divide by the $1.75 rate.
tr.37.71: Divided by 1.75 after adding the $12 fee instead of subtracting it.

M.w: Set up 1.75d + 12 = 54. Subtract 12: 1.75d = 42. Divide by 1.75: d = 24 deliveries. Check: 1.75 × 24 = 42, and 42 + 12 = 54.

M.q: A graph has 'Outdoor temperature (°F)' labeled on the x-axis and 'Heat-related emergency room visits' labeled on the y-axis. Which question is the graph designed to investigate?
o: How does outdoor temperature affect emergency room visits?
How do emergency room visits change from month to month?
How do emergency room visits affect outdoor temperature?
How many patients visit the emergency room each day?
M.w: The x-axis holds the independent variable and the y-axis the dependent variable, so the graph shows how ER visits respond to temperature.

n.1: Change over months would need time on the x-axis, but the x-axis shows temperature.
n.2: This reverses the variables; the y-axis variable is the one that responds.
n.3: A daily count needs no temperature axis; this graph relates two variables.

M.q: A math teacher lists four everyday situations involving two related quantities. Which situation is an example of direct variation?
o: The balance on a $500 gift card after spending $25 per week
The time needed to drive 100 miles at different speeds
Total pay at $22 per hour, with no other pay
A taxi fare of $3 for pickup plus $2.50 per mile
M.w: Direct variation has the form y = kx: zero hours gives zero pay, and doubling the hours doubles the pay (pay = 22h).

n.0: Balance = 500 - 25w is a decreasing linear relationship, not y = kx.
n.1: Time = 100 / speed is inverse variation: doubling the speed halves the time.
n.3: Fare = 2.50m + 3 is linear, but the $3 starting fee means it does not pass through the origin, so it is not direct variation.

M.q: Four race times, in minutes, are listed in different forms. Which list shows the times in descending order (greatest to least)?

n.0: 2.205 is less than 2 1/4 = 2.250, so it must come after 2 1/4.
n.1: This list is in ascending order (least to greatest), the reverse of what is asked.
n.3: 2.205 is not the greatest; having more digits does not make a decimal larger (2.205 < 2.3).

M.q: A clinic records each new patient's blood type (A, B, AB, or O) to help plan its blood supply. Which measure of center can be used to describe these data?
o: The median
The weighted mean
The mode
The mean
M.w: Blood type is categorical data with no numeric values or natural order, so the mode (the most common type) is the only usable measure of center.

n.0: A median needs values that can be put in a meaningful order; A, B, AB and O have none.
n.1: A weighted mean also needs numeric values to multiply by the weights.
n.3: A mean needs numeric values to add, and blood types are categories.

M.q: A provider orders amoxicillin 375 mg by mouth. The pharmacy supplies amoxicillin oral suspension containing 250 mg per 5 mL. How many milliliters should be given?
o: 7.5 mL
3.3 mL
75 mL
1.5 mL
M.w: Desired ÷ have × quantity: 375 ÷ 250 × 5 = 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 mL. As a proportion: 250 mg/5 mL = 375 mg/x, so 250x = 1,875 and x = 7.5 mL.

n.1: This inverts the dose ratio, using 250/375 × 5 instead of 375/250 × 5.
n.2: This divides 375 mg by 5 mL, as if each milliliter held 5 mg.
n.3: This divides the desired dose by the dose on hand but does not multiply by the 5 mL quantity.

M.q: A histogram of household incomes in a town has a tall peak on the left and a long tail stretching to the right. Which statement about the incomes is most likely true?
o: The mean and median are about equal
The distribution is skewed to the left
The mean is greater than the median
The median is greater than the mean
M.w: A long tail to the right is a right (positive) skew. The few very high incomes pull the mean toward the tail, so the mean is greater than the median.

n.0: Mean and median are about equal in a symmetric distribution, not a skewed one.
n.1: Skew is named for the tail, not the peak; the tail here is on the right.
n.3: That relationship fits a left-skewed distribution, where the tail is on the low side.

M.q: The bar graph shows the average wait time at six urgent care clinics. Clinic E's unusually short time pulls the mean of all six below the median, so the director leaves Clinic E out of the report. Select the clinic whose wait time equals the mean of the other five clinics.
M.w: Without Clinic E, the five times are 22, 23, 25, 26 and 34 minutes. Mean = (22 + 23 + 25 + 26 + 34) / 5 = 130 / 5 = 26, which is Clinic D. Dropping the extreme low value raised the mean from about 22.7 (136 / 6) to 26, while the median moved only from 24 to 25: an outlier shifts the mean far more than the median.

n.a: 25 is the median of the remaining five times (22, 23, 25, 26, 34), not the mean. The long 34-minute wait pulls the mean above the median, to 26.
n.b: 34 is the longest wait. It pulls the mean of the five up, but the mean is 26, not 34.
n.c: 22 is the shortest of the remaining five times, well below their mean of 26.
n.e: Clinic E is the value the director left out, so it cannot be the mean of the other five.
n.f: 23 is the value closest to the mean of all six clinics (136 / 6, about 22.7), but that mean still includes Clinic E's 6 minutes. Without it the mean is 26.

M.q: Lena has $70 to spend on a phone case that costs $16 and some charging cables that cost $9.50 each. Ignoring tax, what is the greatest number of cables she can buy along with the case?
M.w: Write 16 + 9.50c ≤ 70. Subtract 16: 9.50c ≤ 54. Divide by 9.50: c ≤ 5.68. She can buy only whole cables, so the greatest number is 5 (5 × 9.50 = 47.50, total $63.50).

n.0: Sign error: this adds the $16 to $70 instead of subtracting it, giving 86 ÷ 9.50 ≈ 9.05.
n.1: This rounds 5.68 up. Six cables cost $57, and $57 + $16 = $73, which is over $70.
n.3: This divides the whole $70 by $9.50 and ignores the $16 case.

M.q: What is the value of (-3) × 4 × (-2) × (-1) ÷ (-6)?
M.w: Multiply left to right: (-3)(4) = -12; (-12)(-2) = 24; (24)(-1) = -24. Then -24 ÷ (-6) = 4. There are four negative signs (an even number), so the result is positive.

n.0: -4 miscounts the negative signs; there are four negatives, an even number, so the result is positive.
n.1: 144 multiplies -24 by -6 instead of dividing.
n.2: -144 multiplies by -6 instead of dividing and also miscounts the signs.

M.q: Kayla completed 0.875 of her required clinical observation hours by the end of October. Which fraction, written in lowest terms, is equivalent to 0.875?
M.w: 0.875 has three decimal places: 875/1,000. The GCF of 875 and 1,000 is 125, so 875/1,000 = 7/8.

n.0: 7/80 = 0.0875, ten times smaller than 0.875.
n.1: 87/100 = 0.87; it drops the thousandths digit instead of converting the full decimal.
n.3: 35/40 equals 0.875, but it is not in lowest terms; 35 and 40 still share a factor of 5.

M.q: A medical assistant counts 23 heartbeats in 20 seconds. At this rate, what is the patient's heart rate in beats per minute? Enter the number of beats per minute.

tr.46: Doubled the 20-second count instead of tripling it.
tr.1.15: Divided 23 by 20 to get beats per second and stopped.

M.w: One minute is 60 seconds, which is 3 × 20 seconds. Heart rate = 23 × 3 = 69 beats per minute.

M.q: A physical therapist records that a patient's forward reach improved by 2 3/8 inches. Write this length as an exact decimal. Enter the number of inches only.

tr.0.375: Gave only the fraction part and dropped the 2 whole inches.

M.w: Divide the fraction part: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Add the whole number: 2 + 0.375 = 2.375 inches.

M.q: A hospital department logged 2,749.5 overtime hours last year. What is 2,749.5 rounded to the nearest hundred?
M.w: The hundreds digit is 7. Look only at the digit to its right (tens), which is 4, so keep 7: 2,700.

n.0: 2,800 rounds in two steps (2,749.5 → 2,750 → 2,800). Round once, using the tens digit.
n.2: 2,750 rounds to the nearest ten, not the nearest hundred.
n.3: 3,000 rounds to the nearest thousand.

M.q: An urgent care clinic bills a $40 visit fee plus $25 for each lab test. A patient's bill came to $165. Which equation can be used to find t, the number of lab tests the patient had?
M.w: Total = fixed fee + rate × quantity, so 25t + 40 = 165. Solving: 25t = 125, so t = 5 lab tests.

n.0: The $40 fee is already part of the $165 bill, so it is subtracted from 165, not added: 25t = 165 - 40.
n.2: This multiplies the visit fee by 25 as well. The $40 is a one-time charge that is added to 25t.
n.3: This swaps the rate and the fixed fee: $25 is charged for each test, and $40 is charged once per visit.

M.q: A medication is given every 6 hours. The first dose was given at 2140 (24-hour clock). At what time is the third dose due, in 12-hour time?
M.w: Second dose: 2140 + 6 h = 0340. Third dose: 0340 + 6 h = 0940, which is 9:40 a.m. The third dose comes two intervals (12 hours) after the first.

n.0: 3:40 a.m. (0340) is the second dose.
n.2: 3:40 p.m. adds three 6-hour intervals (18 h); the third dose is only two intervals after the first.
n.3: 0940 is before noon, so it is 9:40 a.m.; 9:40 p.m. would be written 2140.

M.q: A pie chart shows the blood types of 400 patients. Of these patients, 152 have type O blood. What is the central angle of the type O sector?
M.w: Fraction of the whole: 152 / 400 = 0.38. Central angle = 0.38 x 360° = 136.8°.

n.1: 38 is the percent (38%), not the angle; it must be multiplied by 360° as a decimal.
n.2: 152 is the number of patients, not degrees.
n.3: 0.62 x 360° = 223.2° is the angle for all the patients who are not type O.

M.q: A hospital wants to show what percent of its $2.4 million annual budget goes to each of its five departments. Which display is most appropriate?
o: Histogram
Scatterplot
Circle graph
Line graph
M.w: A circle (pie) graph shows how a whole, here the total budget, is divided into parts, with each sector's size matching its percent.

n.0: A histogram shows the distribution of a numeric variable in intervals, not shares of a total.
n.1: A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numeric variables.
n.3: A line graph shows change over time, and the budget split is for one year.

M.q: To qualify for an honors program, Jordan needs a mean score of at least 85 on five exams. Jordan's first four scores are 78, 91, 84, and 88. What is the lowest score Jordan can earn on the fifth exam and still qualify?

tr.85: the target mean, not the needed score
tr.85.25: the mean of the first four scores

M.w: Total needed = mean x count = 85 x 5 = 425. Current total = 78 + 91 + 84 + 88 = 341. Fifth score = 425 - 341 = 84.

M.q: A patient on a fluid restriction weighed 68.4 kg on Monday and 67.85 kg on Friday. How many kilograms did the patient lose between the two weigh-ins? Enter the number of kilograms only.

tr.1.45: Subtracted the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing.
tr.136.25: Added the weights instead of subtracting.

M.w: Line up the decimal points and write 68.4 as 68.40: 68.40 - 67.85 = 0.55 kg.

M.q: A student simplifies four equations to check how many solutions each one has. Which equation has no solution?
M.w: 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6, so the equation becomes 3x + 6 = 3x + 2. Subtracting 3x leaves 6 = 2, which is false for every x, so there is no solution.

n.1: This becomes 3x + 6 = 2x + 6, which gives x = 0, exactly one solution.
n.2: Subtracting 2x and 2 from both sides gives x = 1, exactly one solution.
n.3: Both sides simplify to 3x + 6, so every value of x works; this equation has infinitely many solutions.

M.q: A rectangular dog run has a perimeter of 68 feet. Its length is 22 feet. A pet owner wants to cover the ground with artificial turf. What is the area of the dog run?
o: 374 ft²
528 ft²
264 ft²
M.w: The two lengths use 2 × 22 = 44 ft. 68 - 44 = 24 ft for the two widths, so width = 12 ft. Area = 22 × 12 = 264 ft².

n.0: This uses 68 ÷ 4 = 17 ft as the width, as if the run were a square.
n.1: This takes the width as 68 - 2(22) = 24 ft, but 24 ft is both widths together.
n.2: This takes the width as 68 - 22 = 46 ft; both lengths must be subtracted, then the rest split between two widths.

M.q: Maya's monthly budget of $2,400 is shown in a pie chart: Rent 35%, Food 15%, Transportation 12.5%, Savings 10%, Other 27.5%. How much more does she budget for rent than for food and transportation combined?
M.w: Amount = percent x total. Rent: 0.35 x 2,400 = $840. Food: 0.15 x 2,400 = $360. Transportation: 0.125 x 2,400 = $300. Food + transportation = $660. Difference: 840 - 660 = $180.

n.1: 840 - 300 = $540 compares rent with transportation only.
n.2: 840 - 360 = $480 compares rent with food only.
n.3: $660 is the food and transportation total, not how much more rent is.

M.q: A nurse started her shift at 6:45 a.m. and clocked out at 7:20 p.m. the same day. How long was she at work?
o: 11 h 35 min
13 h 25 min
12 h 35 min
12 h 25 min
M.w: From 6:45 a.m. to 6:45 p.m. is 12 hours. From 6:45 p.m. to 7:20 p.m. is 15 + 20 = 35 minutes. Total: 12 h 35 min.

n.0: 11 h 35 min borrows an hour twice; only one hour is borrowed to turn 20 minutes into 80.
n.1: 13 h 25 min subtracts the hours (19 - 6 = 13) and then the smaller minute value from the larger (45 - 20) instead of borrowing an hour.
n.3: 12 h 25 min subtracts 20 from 45 minutes; from :45 to :20 of the next hour is 35 minutes.

M.q: In a hospital volunteer program, the ratio of high school volunteers to college volunteers is 3:5, and there are 40 volunteers in total. How many more high school volunteers must join so that the ratio becomes 1:1?
M.w: Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8, so each part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5. High school: 3 × 5 = 15; college: 5 × 5 = 25. For 1:1, the high school group needs 25, so 25 - 15 = 10 must join.

n.1: This subtracts the ratio terms (5 - 3). The actual groups are 15 and 25 volunteers.
n.2: This is the current number of high school volunteers, not the number who must join.
n.3: This is the number of college volunteers, which is the target size of the high school group, not the number who must join.

M.q: Jordan earns $2,850 per month. He puts 12% of his earnings into a retirement account and 8% into a savings account. How much of his monthly earnings is left after both?
M.w: Both are percents of the same $2,850, so they add: 12% + 8% = 20% set aside, leaving 80%. 0.80 × 2,850 = $2,280.

n.0: This subtracts the 12% retirement contribution but not the 8% savings.
n.2: This subtracts the 8% savings but not the 12% retirement contribution.
n.3: This is the 20% set aside, not the amount left.

S.q: A student hypothesizes that an enzyme works faster as temperature rises to 37 °C and works more slowly as temperature rises above 37 °C. The bar graph shows how long the enzyme took to break down the same amount of substrate at each temperature. Select the bar that is inconsistent with the hypothesis.
S.w: A faster enzyme needs less time. The hypothesis predicts times that fall up to 37 °C and rise above it. From 21 to 29 °C the times fall (52, 44, 35 s), but at 33 °C the time jumps to 46 s, longer than at 25 or 29 °C, before dropping to 20 s at 37 °C.
